blocks.text: Real-world analogue: Fossil-bearing desert badlands and exposed geological strata—places such as Dinosaur Provincial Park in Alberta, the Hell Creek badlands, the Painted Desert, and North African fossil beds. Wind and erosion reveal different ages as visible bands. A fossil can be found because a layer is exposed, but exposure also begins its destruction.

Visual translation: The Outer Cache resembles loose scree, wind-cut surface stone, and recently deposited sand where decoys and routing signs are easily replaced. The Working Cache resembles an active dig face with scaffolds, paths, tools, and newly exposed material. The Memory Cache resembles fossil-bearing beds in which continuity marks lie in relationship to the layer around them. The Deep Cache resembles buried strata, compressed bone beds, petroleum-dark shale, or a sealed canyon wall whose contents cannot be exposed without changing them.

World relation: Primarily Continuity and Quiet World logic. Continuity depends on the order and relationship of layers; Quiet practice limits excavation because preservation is not the same as permanent public access.

Connection to newer locations: It directly relates to the Marble Dune Cemetery, Salt Mirror Archive, Glacial Memory Fjord, Redwood Rain Vault, and River of Deferred Reflections. Each is another method of storing history in landscape rather than in a conventional library.

Abstract or metaphorical relation: Memory is stratigraphy, not a pile of interchangeable files. Context is part of the record. Digging deeper can reveal truth, but it can also destroy protection, mix eras, remove provenance, or awaken material a community was not prepared to interpret.
